noteBlocks.md:
A **saprophyte** is an organism that feeds on **dead** material. Saprophytic **fungi and bacteria** do it in three steps, and every step is a marking point.

**1 Secretion.** The fungus or bacterium **secretes enzymes out of its cells** onto the dead material.
**2 Extracellular digestion.** The enzymes **break the large insoluble molecules down outside the cell** — that is exactly what *extracellular* means.
**3 Absorption.** The small **soluble products** are then **absorbed** back into the cells.

noteBlocks.prompt: Digestion by a fungus happens outside its cells, so it is called ______ digestion.
noteBlocks.explain: Extracellular: extra- meaning outside, cellular meaning of the cell. It is the word the scheme lists, and it earns its own mark.

noteBlocks.title: Why outside, and why it matters to everything else
noteBlocks.md: Large molecules such as starch and protein are far too big to cross a cell membrane, and a fungus has no mouth to take them in first. So it turns the problem inside out: send the enzymes to the food instead of bringing the food to the enzymes. What this does for the ecosystem is **recycle nutrients** — carbon, nitrogen and minerals locked up in dead leaves, wood and bodies are released back into the soil where plants can take them up again — and it builds **humus**, the dark, crumbly organic material in soil.

noteBlocks.prompt: Why must a fungus digest its food outside its cells?
options: the molecules are too large to cross the cell membrane
it has no enzymes inside its cells
the soil is too cold inside the cell
noteBlocks.answer: the molecules are too large to cross the cell membrane
noteBlocks.explain: Large molecules cannot cross the membrane, so the enzymes go out to the food instead.

noteBlocks.md: Decomposers are living things, so they decay material fastest when the conditions suit **them**: **warm** (their enzymes work faster, but not so hot that the enzymes are denatured), **moist** (they need water, and enzymes work in solution) and **aerobic** (they respire aerobically, which releases far more energy than anaerobic respiration). Bag **A**, warm and moist with plenty of air, lost **48 g** of its **60 g** in 12 weeks. Bag **C**, warm but waterlogged so the air was excluded, lost only **12 g**. Waterlogging is why peat bogs preserve wood and leaves for thousands of years.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which set of conditions gives the fastest decay?
options: warm, moist and plenty of air
cold, moist and plenty of air
noteBlocks.answer: warm, moist and plenty of air
noteBlocks.explain: All three at once. Take away the warmth, the water or the air and the decomposers slow right down.

noteBlocks.prompt: Bag C fell from 60 g to 48 g over 12 weeks. What was the rate of decomposition, in grams per week?
noteBlocks.explain: (60 − 48) ÷ 12 = 12 ÷ 12 = 1 g per week. Divide by the whole time the experiment ran, not by the gap between two readings — March 2026 examiners said many candidates divided by an incorrect time.

noteBlocks.caption: Eight named processes and one box of air. Every arrow into the air box adds carbon dioxide; only one arrow takes it out.

noteBlocks.md: Only **one** process removes carbon dioxide from the air: **photosynthesis**. Three put it back: **respiration, combustion, decomposition**. The rest move carbon **between organisms** without touching the air at all — **feeding** passes it along a chain, **excretion** and **egestion** pass it to dead material, and **fossilisation** locks it away underground for millions of years until combustion releases it.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which process moves carbon from a dead animal into the soil?
noteBlocks.explain: Decomposition. Fossilisation locks carbon underground instead, and photosynthesis takes it from the air.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q2(b) — respiration in both columns
noteBlocks.md: The question gave a two-column table: processes that **add** carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, and processes that **remove** it. **Many candidates put respiration in both columns.** Respiration only ever produces carbon dioxide — in a plant just as much as in an animal. The reason a plant takes carbon dioxide in during the day is photosynthesis happening faster than respiration, not respiration running backwards.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Carbon Cycle"
noteBlocks.why: The whole cycle drawn arrow by arrow in a few minutes. Watch it, then answer the question underneath without looking back at the diagram.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
noteBlocks.explain: Photosynthesis, and only photosynthesis. The other three all release carbon dioxide back into the air.

steps.decision: Start with the verb the scheme lists: secrete. 'It puts enzymes on the leaf' will usually be accepted, but 'it eats the leaf' is not a description of anything the fungus can do.

steps.working: The enzymes digest the large insoluble molecules in the leaf outside the fungus — extracellular digestion.
steps.decision: Name where the digestion happens. This is the point the March 2026 report says candidates could not describe.

steps.working: The small soluble products are absorbed into the fungus.
steps.decision: Finish with absorption. Three verbs, three marks: secrete, digest, absorb.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The fungus secretes enzymes out of its cells onto the dead leaf. The enzymes digest the large insoluble molecules in the leaf outside the fungus, which is extracellular digestion. The small soluble products of that digestion are then absorbed into the fungus.

items.stem: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?
items.skill: One arrow out, three arrows in

options.text: photosynthesis
options.feedback: Photosynthesis, and nothing else on this cycle. Green plants take carbon dioxide in and lock the carbon into glucose.

options.text: respiration
options.feedback: Respiration always produces carbon dioxide. Summer 2025 examiners reported it written in both columns of the table.

options.text: combustion
options.feedback: Burning a fuel releases carbon dioxide. It is one of the three that add.

options.text: decomposition
options.feedback: Decomposers respire as they break dead material down, so decomposition adds carbon dioxide.

items.stem: Where does a saprophytic fungus digest its food?

options.text: outside its cells, on the dead material
options.feedback: Extracellular digestion. The enzymes go out to the food, because the food cannot come in.

options.text: inside its cells, after swallowing it
options.feedback: A fungus has no mouth and cannot swallow. It secretes enzymes onto the food and absorbs the products.

options.text: in a stomach at the base of the hypha
options.feedback: Fungi have no digestive system at all. Everything happens outside the cell.

options.text: in the soil, once the material has dissolved by itself
options.feedback: Dead leaves do not dissolve on their own. The fungus has to secrete enzymes to break them down.

items.stem: In which conditions would leaf litter decay fastest?

options.text: warm, moist, plenty of air
options.feedback: All three together. Decomposers are living organisms, so they work fastest when their own conditions are right.

options.text: cold, moist, plenty of air
options.feedback: Cold slows the decomposers' enzymes, so decay is slower. That is why food keeps in a fridge.

options.text: warm, waterlogged, no air
options.feedback: Waterlogging drives the air out, so the decomposers cannot respire aerobically and decay is very slow.

options.text: hot, dry, plenty of air
options.feedback: Without water the decomposers cannot grow and their enzymes cannot work in solution.

options.text: an organism that feeds on dead material
options.feedback: Dead material — that is what sapro- means. Fungi and bacteria are the saprophytes on this specification.

options.text: an organism that feeds on a living host and harms it
options.feedback: That is a parasite. A saprophyte feeds on material that is already dead.

options.text: an organism that makes its own food from light
options.feedback: That is a producer. Fungi have no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise.

options.text: an animal that eats other animals' remains
options.feedback: A scavenger swallows its food. A saprophyte digests it outside its body and absorbs the products.

options.feedback: 12 g lost ÷ 12 weeks = 1 g per week.
Divided by the 4-week gap between readings instead of the 12 weeks the experiment ran. March 2026 examiners named this exact error.
That is the total mass lost, not a rate. A rate needs the division by time.
That is the mass left at the end. Start by subtracting to find how much was lost.

options.feedback: True, but it answers a different question. March 2026 examiners reported candidates giving the fastest conditions when the trend was asked for.

options.text: Environment C decomposed the slowest.
options.feedback: A single comparison is not a trend. A trend says what happens as one variable changes.

options.text: The mass changed over the twelve weeks.
options.feedback: 'Changed' gives no direction. Say that the mass decreased as time increased.

parts.stem: What does respiration do to the amount of carbon dioxide in the air?

options.text: adds carbon dioxide to the air
options.feedback: Always adds, in plants as well as animals. Respiration has only one direction.

options.text: removes carbon dioxide from the air
options.feedback: Respiration produces carbon dioxide; it never takes it in. Summer 2025 examiners found it entered in both columns of the table.

options.text: both, depending on whether it happens in a plant or an animal
options.feedback: Plants respire exactly as animals do, releasing carbon dioxide. It is photosynthesis that takes carbon dioxide in.

options.text: neither: it moves carbon between organisms
options.feedback: Feeding moves carbon between organisms. Respiration puts it into the air as carbon dioxide.

scheme.for: adds carbon dioxide to the air
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 B1 F Q2(b): many candidates put respiration in both columns.

hints: Write the word equation for respiration and look at the right-hand side.
parts.workedSolution: It adds carbon dioxide to the air.

parts.stem: What does photosynthesis do to the amount of carbon dioxide in the air?

options.text: adds carbon dioxide to the air
options.feedback: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide up, so it removes it. Look at which side of the word equation it appears on.

options.text: removes carbon dioxide from the air
options.feedback: The only arrow on the cycle that takes carbon dioxide out of the air.

options.text: both, depending on the time of day
options.feedback: Photosynthesis stops in the dark, but it never reverses. At night the plant only respires, which adds carbon dioxide.

options.text: neither
options.feedback: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so the process takes it out of the air.

scheme.for: removes carbon dioxide from the air

hints: Carbon dioxide is a raw material, so it is used up.
parts.workedSolution: It removes carbon dioxide from the air.

parts.stem: What does decomposition do to the amount of carbon dioxide in the air?

options.text: adds carbon dioxide to the air
options.feedback: The decomposers respire as they break the dead material down, so carbon dioxide is released.

options.text: removes carbon dioxide from the air
options.feedback: Only photosynthesis removes it. Decomposers are not plants and have no chlorophyll.

options.text: nothing: it only returns minerals to the soil
options.feedback: It does return minerals, but the decomposers also respire, and that releases carbon dioxide.

options.text: it locks carbon away underground
options.feedback: That is fossilisation, which happens when dead material is buried before it can decompose.

scheme.for: adds carbon dioxide to the air

hints: Decomposers are living organisms, so they respire.
parts.workedSolution: It adds carbon dioxide to the air, because the decomposers respire as they feed.

context.setting: Mould growing over a slice of dropped bread in a bin

parts.stem: Describe how the mould obtains its food from the bread.

accepted: the mould secretes enzymes out onto the bread, the enzymes digest the large molecules outside the mould's cells, and the small soluble products are absorbed into the mould

scheme.for: secretes enzymes onto the bread
the enzymes digest the material outside the cells (extracellular digestion)
the soluble products are absorbed

hints: Three verbs, in order.
A mould has no mouth, so where does the digestion have to happen?
parts.workedSolution: The mould secretes enzymes out of its cells onto the bread. The enzymes digest the large insoluble molecules outside the mould — extracellular digestion. The small soluble products are then absorbed into the mould's cells.

commonErrors.feedback: A saprophyte cannot take food in first: the molecules are too large. It secretes enzymes onto the food and absorbs the products afterwards.

parts.stem: State one way in which decomposers are important to an ecosystem.

accepted: they recycle nutrients back into the soil so plants can use them again

scheme.for: they recycle nutrients / release minerals back into the soil for plants / form humus

hints: What happens to the carbon and nitrogen in a dead leaf?
parts.workedSolution: They recycle nutrients: the minerals locked up in dead material are released back into the soil, where plants can absorb them again. They also form humus.

parts.stem: Describe the overall trend shown by the results for all three environments.

accepted: in every environment the mass decreased as time increased, so leaf litter was being broken down throughout the twelve weeks

scheme.for: in all three environments the mass of leaf litter decreased as time increased
scheme.examinerNote: March 2026 B1 Q5(b)(i): many candidates named the conditions for fastest decomposition instead of describing the overall trend.

The question says all three, so one sentence has to cover all three.

commonErrors.feedback: That names the fastest environment, which is a different question. The trend is what happens to the mass in every environment as the weeks go by.

Calculate the decomposition rate in environment C over the 12 weeks, in grams per week.

divides by the full 12 weeks
= 1 g per week

hints: Subtract, then divide by the time the experiment ran.
The readings were taken every 4 weeks, but the question asks over the whole 12.
parts.workedSolution: Mass lost = 60 − 48 = 12 g. Rate = 12 ÷ 12 = 1 g per week.

commonErrors.feedback: Divided by 4, the gap between readings, rather than by the 12 weeks the question names. Read the time interval out of the question before you divide.

parts.stem: Explain why environment C (warm, waterlogged, no air) lost less mass than environment A (warm, moist, plenty of air).

accepted: environment C was waterlogged so there was very little oxygen, the decomposers could not respire aerobically, so they released less energy and grew and reproduced more slowly and broke the leaves down more slowly

scheme.for: C was waterlogged, so there was very little oxygen (it was anaerobic)
the decomposers could not respire aerobically
so they released less energy, grew and reproduced more slowly, and broke down less of the leaf litter

hints: Both were warm, so temperature cannot be the answer.
What do the decomposers need that a waterlogged pond bottom does not have?
parts.workedSolution: Both bags were warm, so the difference is the air. Environment C was waterlogged, so there was very little oxygen and conditions were anaerobic. The decomposers could not respire aerobically, so they released much less energy, grew and reproduced more slowly, and broke down far less of the leaf litter in the same twelve weeks.

commonErrors.feedback: Both environments were warm; the stem says so. The difference between them is the oxygen, not the temperature.

Environment A fell from 60 g to 12 g.

hints: Percentage lost = mass lost ÷ starting mass × 100.

parts.stem: Suggest why grass clippings sealed in an airtight plastic sack rot far more slowly, and smell unpleasant when the sack is opened.

accepted: sealing the sack keeps oxygen out, so the decomposers have to respire anaerobically, which releases less energy so decay is slow and produces different, smelly products

scheme.for: the sealed sack keeps oxygen out
so the decomposers have to respire anaerobically
anaerobic respiration releases much less energy, so they work slowly, and it produces different products that smell
accept: names a smelly product such as an acid or a gas

hints: What has been taken away by sealing the bag?
Which kind of respiration is left, and what does it release?
parts.workedSolution: Sealing the sack keeps oxygen out, so the decomposers cannot respire aerobically and have to respire anaerobically instead. Anaerobic respiration releases far less energy, so the decomposers grow and reproduce slowly and the clippings rot slowly. It also produces different products, which is why the sack smells when it is opened.

commonErrors.feedback: A sealed sack of grass clippings is damp, not dry. What it lacks is oxygen.

parts.stem: One carbon atom travels through the cycle. Put these five stages in the order in which they happen, starting in the air.

items: The carbon atom is in a molecule of carbon dioxide in the air
A green plant takes it in and photosynthesis builds it into glucose
A rabbit eats the plant, so the atom moves along the food chain
The rabbit dies and decomposers feed on its body
The decomposers respire and the atom returns to the air as carbon dioxide

scheme.for: photosynthesis takes the atom out of the air into the plant
feeding moves it from the plant into the rabbit
death and decomposition move it into the decomposers
respiration by the decomposers returns it to the air

hints: Carbon can only leave the air by one route.
It can only return to the air by respiration, combustion or decomposition.
parts.workedSolution: The atom starts as carbon dioxide in the air. Photosynthesis builds it into glucose in a green plant. A rabbit eats the plant, so the atom passes along the food chain. The rabbit dies and decomposers feed on its body. The decomposers respire, and the atom returns to the air as carbon dioxide.

commonErrors.feedback: Respiration only ever returns carbon to the air, so it belongs at the end of this journey and not at the start.

context.setting: A sealed glass jar containing a growing plant, left in the light and then in the dark

parts.stem:
A small plant is sealed in a glass jar and left in bright light. The carbon dioxide concentration inside the jar falls.
Explain why.

accepted: the plant is photosynthesising faster than it is respiring, so it uses up carbon dioxide more quickly than it produces it and the concentration falls

any: greater than the rate of respiration

scheme.for: in bright light the plant photosynthesises faster than it respires
so carbon dioxide is used up faster than it is produced and the concentration falls
reject: the plant does not respire in the light

hints: The plant is doing both things at once.
Which one is winning?
parts.workedSolution: In bright light the plant photosynthesises faster than it respires. Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and respiration produces it, so carbon dioxide is being used up faster than it is being made and its concentration in the jar falls.

pattern.regex: does not respire|stops respiring|plants do not respire

commonErrors.feedback: Plants respire every hour of every day, light or dark. In the light photosynthesis is simply faster, so the net movement of carbon dioxide is inwards.

parts.stem:
The jar is then moved into complete darkness and the carbon dioxide concentration rises.
Explain why.

accepted: in the dark the plant cannot photosynthesise but it still respires, so carbon dioxide is produced and nothing uses it up

scheme.for: in the dark there is no light, so photosynthesis stops
the plant continues to respire, releasing carbon dioxide, and nothing is now using it up

hints: Which of the two processes needs light?
parts.workedSolution: Photosynthesis needs light, so in complete darkness it stops. Respiration does not need light and continues, releasing carbon dioxide. With nothing using the carbon dioxide up, its concentration in the jar rises.

context.setting: A body of a man preserved for two thousand years in an Irish peat bog

parts.stem:
Bodies buried in peat bogs are sometimes found almost undecayed after two thousand years.
Suggest two features of a peat bog that explain this.

accepted: the bog is waterlogged so there is almost no oxygen for the decomposers, and it is cold, which slows their enzymes down

scheme.for: any two from: waterlogged, so almost no oxygen and decomposers cannot respire aerobically / cold, so the decomposers' enzymes work slowly / acidic, which kills or inhibits many decomposers — [1] each

hints: Think of the three conditions decay needs, and which ones a bog fails.
parts.workedSolution: A peat bog is waterlogged, so there is almost no oxygen and the decomposers cannot respire aerobically; and it is cold, so their enzymes work very slowly. (Peat is also acidic, which inhibits many decomposers.)

parts.stem: Explain why a farmer turns a compost heap over with a fork every few weeks.

accepted: turning the heap mixes air into it, so the decomposers have oxygen and can respire aerobically, which makes them work faster and the compost forms more quickly

scheme.for: turning mixes air, and so oxygen, into the heap
so the decomposers can respire aerobically and work faster, and the material decays more quickly

hints: What runs out in the middle of a heap that is never turned?
parts.workedSolution: Turning the heap mixes air into the middle of it, where the oxygen would otherwise be used up. With oxygen available the decomposers can respire aerobically, release much more energy, grow and reproduce faster, and so break the material down more quickly.

commonErrors.feedback: A working compost heap is warm, and warmth speeds decay. Turning it is about letting air in.

hints: Start where the carbon came from, and finish where it goes back to.
Three verbs earn three separate points: secrete, digest, absorb.
parts.workedSolution: The carbon in the leaf came from carbon dioxide in the air, taken in by the oak tree and built into glucose by photosynthesis. Once the leaf falls, saprophytic fungi and bacteria feed on it. They secrete enzymes out onto the leaf, the enzymes digest its large insoluble molecules outside their cells — extracellular digestion — and the small soluble products are absorbed into the decomposers. The decomposers respire, and much of the carbon is released back into the air as carbon dioxide. Some becomes humus in the soil, and the minerals released are recycled and taken up by plants. The leaf disappears quickly because the woodland floor is moist, has air in it and warms up in the spring, which is exactly what the decomposers need.

commonErrors.feedback: Fungi and bacteria have no mouth. They secrete enzymes onto the leaf, digest it outside their cells and absorb the products — three separate points.
Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the air; respiration puts it back. Reversing them undoes the whole cycle.

findTheMistake.stem:
Dáire is asked to complete a table: one column for processes that ADD carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, one for processes that REMOVE it. [3]
His answer:
studentWorking: He explained: 'plants take in carbon dioxide when they respire in the light.'
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: **Respiration appears in both columns.** Respiration only ever *produces* carbon dioxide — in a plant exactly as in an animal. The explanation in line 3 is where the error comes from: a plant in the light does take carbon dioxide in, but that is **photosynthesis** happening faster than respiration, not respiration working in reverse. Decomposition is also missing from the adding column.
correction: A plant in the light takes carbon dioxide in because photosynthesis is faster than respiration, not because respiration reverses.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark from three, and a right answer written beside a wrong one earns nothing under the listing rule — so the removing column scored zero even though photosynthesis was in it. The habit that fixes this is to write the word equation for respiration in the margin before you fill the table in: glucose plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water. Carbon dioxide is on the right, so respiration can only ever add.

prompts.prompt: Describe how a saprophytic fungus feeds, in three steps.
prompts.answer: It secretes enzymes out of its cells onto the dead material; the enzymes digest it outside the cells (extracellular digestion); the small soluble products are absorbed.

prompts.prompt: What is a saprophyte, and what does it form in the soil?
prompts.answer: An organism that feeds on dead material. Saprophytic fungi and bacteria recycle nutrients and form humus.

prompts.prompt: Which three conditions make decay fastest?
prompts.answer: Warm, moist and aerobic (plenty of oxygen).

prompts.prompt: Which processes ADD carbon dioxide to the air, and which REMOVES it?
prompts.answer: Adds: respiration, combustion, decomposition. Removes: photosynthesis, and nothing else. Respiration never goes in the removing column.

prompts.prompt: Name the eight processes the specification lists in the carbon cycle.
prompts.answer: Photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, fossilisation, feeding, excretion, egestion and decomposition.

prompts.prompt: Why does a plant take carbon dioxide in during the day but give it out at night?
prompts.answer: It photosynthesises and respires all the time. In the light photosynthesis is faster, so carbon dioxide moves in overall; in the dark photosynthesis stops and only respiration continues, so carbon dioxide moves out.

prompts.prompt: How do you calculate a rate of decomposition in grams per week?
prompts.answer: Subtract the final mass from the starting mass, then divide by the total number of weeks the experiment ran — not by the gap between readings.

prompts.prompt: Why is decay very slow in a waterlogged soil or a sealed bag?
prompts.answer: There is almost no oxygen, so the decomposers cannot respire aerobically; they release much less energy, grow slowly and break material down slowly.
